findings.claim: serving the approximately 430,000 Sikhs in Britain
findings.truth: 430,000 is close to the 2011 census figure (423,158 in England and Wales). The 2021 census recorded 524,140 Sikhs in England and Wales and the 2022 Scottish census 10,988, giving about 535,000 in Britain.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Sikhism in the United Kingdom (2021/2022 census tables)

findings.claim: the largest gurdwara outside India — which can accommodate over 3,000 worshippers
findings.truth: Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha, Southall is documented as the largest Sikh place of worship in London (and so in Britain), with a capacity of 3,000. The 'largest outside India' claim is a press line, not a sourced fact, and 'over 3,000' overstates the recorded capacity.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha, Southall; Wikipedia, Sikhism in the United Kingdom

findings.claim: There is no distinction between where men and women sit in the prayer hall of a gurdwara
findings.truth: Many gurdwaras seat men on one side and women on the other. The division is not compulsory and designs vary, but it is common. Equality is kept because both sides sit the same distance from, and at the same level below, the Guru Granth Sahib.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Gurdwara (darbar seating)

findings.claim: The Sikh flag — a triangular dark blue pennant with the Khanda symbol — flown outside every gurdwara.
findings.truth: The Nishan Sahib flown at gurdwaras worldwide is normally saffron. Dark blue (surmai) is the Nihang usage. The lesson body already says saffron, so the flashcard contradicts the content and teaches the wrong default answer.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Nishan Sahib; internal contradiction with content_html

findings.claim: The Sikh flag — a triangular dark blue pennant bearing the Khanda symbol — flown outside every gurdwara.
findings.truth: Same error as F4: the Nishan Sahib is normally saffron; dark blue is the Nihang variant.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Nishan Sahib; internal contradiction with content_html

findings.claim: Practice question 3 is set as '2 marks — State / Give' ('State two roles of the gurdwara...').
findings.truth: This paper sets two five-part questions per religion with marks of 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12. There is no 2-mark question. The second short part is 1 mark for one item.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments (line 269) and 4.4.1 (lines 1826-1832)

findings.claim: Practice question 3 is set as '2 marks — State / Give' ('Give two reasons why langar is served as vegetarian food.').
findings.truth: No 2-mark question exists on this paper. Marks are 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments (line 269) and 4.4.1 (lines 1826-1832)

findings.claim: The mark scheme requires a named source — a Sikh scriptural reference or a named Guru's action is sufficient.
findings.truth: This is an invented mark-scheme claim. What is verifiable is that the 6-mark question itself instructs the student to refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1; house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Practice question 3 is set as '2 marks — State / Give' ('State two ways in which Vaisakhi is celebrated...').
findings.truth: No 2-mark question exists on this paper. Marks are 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments (line 269) and 4.4.1 (lines 1826-1832)

findings.claim: Examiners reward this distinction.
findings.truth: A fabricated examiner claim. The distinction between Naam Karan and Amrit Sanskar is worth making, but no examiner statement supports the sentence.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: These specific named sources take your answer into the top band.
findings.truth: A fabricated mark-scheme claim. Naming a source does not by itself place an answer in the top band; the question simply instructs the student to refer to a source.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1; house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: It was built under the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan Dev, and completed in 1604.
findings.truth: Guru Arjan began construction in 1581 and the building was completed in 1589. 1604 is the year Guru Arjan installed the first copy of the Adi Granth inside it, not the year the building was finished.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Golden Temple (construction timeline; Adi Granth installed 16 August 1604)

findings.claim: Bandi Chhor Divas ... commemorating Guru Hargobind's release from imprisonment at Gwalior Fort in 1619 (given in the dfn data-def and in the glossary).
findings.truth: The date is contested. Sikh tradition, BBC Bitesize and most GCSE textbooks give 1619; academic accounts summarised on Wikipedia put the release at 1611 or 1612. Options: (a) leave 1619, the date a student will meet in every textbook and will not be penalised for; (b) drop the year from the dfn and the glossary so no contested date is asserted. My recommendation is (a) leave it — no date is required by the specification, and changing it would put the lesson out of step with every other resource the student uses.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Bandi Chhor Divas ('the year of his release appears to have been either 1611 or 1612')

findings.claim: the martyrdom anniversaries of Guru Arjan Dev and Guru Tegh Bahadur (who were executed for refusing to convert to Islam — martyred for the right of religious freedom)
findings.truth: Accurate for Guru Tegh Bahadur. For Guru Arjan the motive is disputed: Jahangir's own memoir gives his influence and his blessing of the rebel prince Khusrau as reasons, while also recording a conversion demand. Historians split between religious and political readings. Not worth an edit at GCSE level, but the sentence states one contested reading as settled fact.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Guru Arjan (competing accounts; Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri)

findings.claim: Practice question 3 is set as '2 marks — State / Give' ('State two of the five Ks...').
findings.truth: No 2-mark question exists on this paper. Marks are 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments (line 269) and 4.4.1 (lines 1826-1832)

findings.claim: After taking amrit, the initiate receives the five Ks (Panj Kakars)
findings.truth: The five Ks are not handed over after the ceremony. The Sikh Rehat Maryada requires the candidate to be wearing all five Ks before the ceremony begins.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Amrit Sanskar, citing the Sikh Rehat Maryada ('The person to become Amritdhari must wear the five holy symbols')

findings.claim: The mark scheme rewards students who distinguish amritdhari and sahajdhari perspectives.
findings.truth: A fabricated mark-scheme claim. The verifiable fact is that the subject content names the different perspectives of sahajdhari and amritdhari Sikhs as something students must study.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.7.2 (line 1141); house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Mark schemes reward students who distinguish amritdhari and sahajdhari perspectives.
findings.truth: Same fabricated mark-scheme claim as F17, repeated in the exam tip.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.7.2 (line 1141); house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: In the UK, the right to carry a kirpan is legally protected as a religious practice for initiated Sikhs.
findings.truth: The Criminal Justice Act 1988 s.139(5)(b) gives a defence of having a bladed article in a public place 'for religious reasons'. The defence turns on religious reason, not on proof of initiation, so 'for initiated Sikhs' overstates the legal test. Not examinable content, so recorded only.
findings.evidence: Criminal Justice Act 1988 s.139(5)(b)

findings.claim: Unlike Hindu temples, the Golden Temple was built with four doors
findings.truth: Four entrances are not unique to the Golden Temple; many Hindu temples are built with four entrances. The Sikh point stands on its own meaning (open to all four directions) without the comparison.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Golden Temple (four entrances symbolise equality)

summary: All four lessons carry a practice question set at 2 marks, which this paper never sets (1, 1, 4, 6, 12 only), plus four fabricated mark-scheme or examiner claims across lessons 2-4. Factual fixes: the UK Sikh population is a 2011 figure, the Southall gurdwara claim and capacity are overstated, the Nishan Sahib is described as dark blue in the lesson 1 flashcard and glossary while the body says saffron, the Golden Temple completion year confuses the 1589 building with the 1604 installation of the scripture, and lesson 4 says the five Ks are received after amrit when the code of conduct requires them to be worn beforehand.
